title: Basic Patterns & Anchors ⚓
description: Match literal text, start/end of line anchors, and the wildcard dot.

slides.title: Literal Characters & The Dot 🅰️
slides.content:
## The Simplest Pattern

Most characters in regex match themselves: `cat` matches "cat". The **dot** (`.`) is the exception – it matches **any single character** except newline.

- `c.t` matches "cat", "cot", "cut", "c9t", etc.
- `..` matches any two characters.

To match a literal dot, escape it: `\.`

slides.title: Anchors: ^ and $ 🎯
slides.content:
## Pin to Start or End

- `^` – matches the **start** of a line.
- `$` – matches the **end** of a line.

Thus:
- `^Hello` – lines that begin with "Hello".
- `world$` – lines that end with "world".
- `^$` – empty lines.

Anchor doesn't consume characters, it asserts position.

quizData.question: What regex matches empty lines?
quizData.explanation: `^$` matches start immediately followed by end, i.e., a line with nothing in between.

slides.title: Escaping Special Characters 🛡️
slides.content:
## When You Need a Literal Dot or Star

These characters have special meaning in regex: `. ^ $ * + ? { } [ ] \ | ( )`

To match them literally, prefix with a backslash `\`. Example: `\$` matches a dollar sign, `\.` matches a period.

Inside `grep -E`, you need double backslashes only if the shell interprets them. Single backslash works inside quotes.

slides.content: Use single quotes around your grep pattern to prevent the shell from interpreting `$`, `\`, and other special characters before grep sees them.
